questions.stem: A 76 year old man has 2 years of slowly progressive breathlessness and a dry cough. He worked as a boilermaker in a naval dockyard from 1965 to 1990. His oxygen saturation is 93% breathing air. He has reduced chest expansion and fine end-inspiratory crackles at both bases. His chest X-ray shows lower zone reticular shadowing and bilateral calcified pleural plaques.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Lower zone interstitial fibrosis with pleural plaques after decades of dockyard work is asbestosis. Pleural plaques separate it from idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: fine end-inspiratory crackles at both bases
steps.x: Occupational exposure + lower zone fibrosis + **pleural plaques** (the exposure marker).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Asbestos-related interstitial fibrosis: **asbestosis**.

elim: Affects coal miners and gives upper zone nodules.
Follows exposure to birds or mould and favours the upper zones.
Looks similar, but the pleural plaques and dockyard work point to asbestos.
Gives bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, often in younger patients.

steps.x: **A. Asbestosis.** Plaques + lower zone fibrosis + dockyard/insulation work = asbestosis.

questions.stem: A 72 year old retired lagger has 3 years of worsening exertional breathlessness. He fitted asbestos insulation to pipes for 20 years. His fingers are clubbed and there are fine crackles at both lung bases. His oxygen saturation is 94% breathing air. A chest X-ray is requested.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on his chest X-ray?
o: Lower zone linear fibrosis with pleural plaques
Upper zone nodules with eggshell hilar calcification
questions.e: Asbestosis gives linear interstitial fibrosis predominantly in the lower lobes, often with pleural plaques. Silicosis and coal dust favour the upper zones.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: fitted asbestos insulation to pipes for 20 years
fine crackles at both lung bases
steps.x: Asbestos insulation, clubbing, basal crackles = **asbestosis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Lower zone linear fibrosis with pleural plaques.**
**C. Lower zone linear fibrosis with pleural plaques.** Asbestos = lower zones; silica and coal = upper zones.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman has 2 months of right-sided chest pain, breathlessness and 7 kg weight loss. She has never worked with asbestos but washed her husband's overalls when he was a shipyard lagger in the 1970s. Her brother died of a pleural cancer. She has stony dull percussion at the right base. Chest X-ray (see item resources).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Domestic asbestos exposure, a very long latent period, chest pain, weight loss and a unilateral effusion suggest mesothelioma, which can run in families.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: brother died of a pleural cancer
steps.x: Domestic exposure decades ago + chest pain + weight loss + unilateral effusion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Malignant pleural mesothelioma.**

elim: Plaques are asymptomatic and do not cause effusion or weight loss.
Gives bilateral effusions without weight loss or chest wall pain.
She has no fever or infection.
Possible, but asbestos exposure and family history point to mesothelioma.

steps.x: **C. Malignant pleural mesothelioma.** Mesothelioma: long latency, chest pain, weight loss, unilateral effusion; even domestic exposure counts.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has a chest X-ray before a knee operation. It shows calcified pleural plaques on both hemidiaphragms and the lower lateral chest walls. He is well and not breathless. He remembers cutting asbestos cement sheets when working on a building site as a young man.
questions.q: When did his asbestos exposure most likely occur?
questions.e: Pleural plaques indicate asbestos exposure 20 to 40 years earlier; asbestos disease has a very long latency.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Calcified plaques = old exposure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Latency for plaques: **20 to 40 years ago**.

elim: Far too short a latent period.
Still too short for calcified plaques.
Plaques do not form this quickly.

steps.x: **C. 20 to 40 years ago.** Asbestos disease has a very long latency: plaques mark exposure 20 to 40 years earlier.

questions.stem: A 69 year old retired electrician who worked in old office blocks in the 1970s has a routine medical. He has no breathlessness or cough. His chest is clear on examination and his oxygen saturation is 98% breathing air. His lung function is normal. A chest X-ray is taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on his chest X-ray?
o: Calcified plaques on the diaphragm and lower lateral chest wall
questions.e: Pleural plaques are usually asymptomatic, calcified, in the lower zones on the lower lateral chest wall and diaphragm, with no consolidation.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Past asbestos exposure, no symptoms, normal lungs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Calcified plaques on the diaphragm and lower lateral chest wall.**

elim: He would usually be breathless; suggests malignancy.

steps.x: **B. Calcified plaques on the diaphragm and lower lateral chest wall.** Asymptomatic + exposure = pleural plaques (lower zones, diaphragm).

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has 2 months of haemoptysis and 6 kg weight loss. He fitted asbestos lagging in a shipyard for 25 years and has smoked 30 cigarettes a day for 45 years. His oxygen saturation is 95% breathing air. CT shows a 4 cm spiculated mass at the right hilum with enlarged mediastinal nodes and no pleural thickening.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Asbestos and smoking combined markedly increase the risk of lung cancer; a spiculated hilar mass with nodes is bronchial carcinoma, not pleural mesothelioma.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: spiculated mass at the right hilum
steps.x: Asbestos + heavy smoking + hilar mass, pleura spared.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bronchial carcinoma.**

elim: Diffuse lower zone fibrosis, not a hilar mass.
Arises from the pleura; there is no pleural thickening.
Benign, asymptomatic and do not form masses.
Usually upper lobe cavities with fever and night sweats.

steps.x: **B. Bronchial carcinoma.** Asbestos + smoking = big lung cancer risk; pleural tumour = mesothelioma.

questions.stem: A 73 year old former pipe fitter has 3 months of increasing breathlessness and 8 kg weight loss. He has coughed up streaks of blood twice. CT shows irregular nodular thickening of the left pleura with a moderate effusion. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air.
questions.q: Which additional symptom is he most likely to report?
o: Episodic wheeze triggered by cold air
Painful swollen joints of the hands
questions.e: Mesothelioma presents with breathlessness, pleural effusion, weight loss, haemoptysis and chest pain, often a dull ache from chest wall invasion.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: nodular thickening of the left pleura
steps.x: Pipe fitter + weight loss + nodular pleural thickening = **mesothelioma**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Persistent dull chest wall pain.**
**E. Persistent dull chest wall pain.** Mesothelioma: breathless, effusion, weight loss, haemoptysis, chest pain.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man who sprayed asbestos insulation in the 1960s has 6 weeks of right-sided chest pain and breathlessness. His oxygen saturation is 94% breathing air. His right base is dull to percussion. A CT chest with contrast is arranged to look for the classic complication of his exposure.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on CT?
o: Hyperdense pleural mass anteriorly on the right
Pulmonary emboli in both main arteries
questions.e: Mesothelioma, the classic asbestos complication with a very long latency, may show a right-sided anterior hyperdense pleural-based structure on CT.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Decades-old exposure + one-sided chest pain and dullness = **mesothelioma**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hyperdense pleural mass anteriorly on the right.**

elim: Gives acute breathlessness without pleural disease.

steps.x: **D. Hyperdense pleural mass anteriorly on the right.** Mesothelioma on CT: pleural-based mass or thickening, often right-sided.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man is told his chest X-ray shows bilateral calcified pleural plaques. He worked as a ship's engineer 30 years ago. He is well, a non-smoker and his lung function is normal. He is anxious that he has cancer.
questions.q: Which is the most likely significance of these plaques?
o: A marker of past exposure with no malignant change
A premalignant lesion that becomes mesothelioma
questions.e: Pleural plaques form when fibres irritate the pleura; they are a benign marker of past exposure, not premalignant, and are not linked to a higher cancer risk.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Well, normal lungs, calcified plaques.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **A marker of past exposure with no malignant change.**

elim: Plaques do not undergo malignant change.
Plaques are pleural; asbestosis is interstitial fibrosis.
Metastases are not calcified plaques in a well man.

steps.x: **A. A marker of past exposure with no malignant change.** Plaques are benign: no malignant change, no follow-up.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man has asbestosis confirmed on CT with bilateral pleural plaques. He has had several jobs during his life and the respiratory team takes a detailed occupational history. His oxygen saturation is 93% breathing air.
questions.q: Which previous job is most likely to have caused his disease?
questions.e: Occupational exposure in construction, shipbuilding and insulation work is the most important risk factor for asbestos-related lung disease.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Asbestosis: which job involved asbestos?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Shipyard insulation fitter.**

elim: Coal dust causes coal worker's pneumoconiosis.

steps.x: **E. Shipyard insulation fitter.** Asbestos jobs: shipbuilding, construction, insulation, lagging, demolition.

questions.stem: A 70 year old former demolition worker has 18 months of progressive breathlessness and a dry cough. He knocked down buildings lined with asbestos boards for 25 years. His oxygen saturation is 94% breathing air. His CT shows lower lobe interstitial fibrosis and pleural plaques.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his chest?
o: Bronchial breathing at the left base
Coarse crackles that clear on coughing
Fine bibasal crackles with reduced chest expansion
questions.e: Asbestosis gives progressive breathlessness, cough, fine bibasal crackles and reduced chest expansion from stiff, fibrotic lungs.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Asbestos exposure + lower lobe fibrosis = **asbestosis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Fine bibasal crackles with reduced chest expansion.**

elim: Suggests secretions, as in bronchiectasis or infection.

steps.x: **C. Fine bibasal crackles with reduced chest expansion.** Asbestosis signs: fine bibasal crackles, reduced chest expansion, clubbing.

questions.stem: A 58 year old non-smoker worked for 3 years in the 1980s stripping blue asbestos from old trains. He is well. He asks which cancer is most specifically linked to his exposure, as he has read that asbestos causes several diseases with a long delay.
questions.q: Which malignancy is most specifically associated with asbestos exposure?
questions.e: Mesothelioma is the rare but classic asbestos-related cancer, with a very long latency; nearly all cases follow asbestos exposure.

steps.x: This asks what is going on. Name the condition or finding from the stem before looking at the options.
Non-smoker with blue asbestos exposure: the signature cancer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Malignant mesothelioma.**

elim: Linked to hepatitis B or C and cirrhosis.
Mainly smoking-related; asbestos raises lung cancer risk, but mesothelioma is the specific one.

steps.x: **C. Malignant mesothelioma.** The cancer that means asbestos: mesothelioma.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man has CT changes of lower lobe interstitial fibrosis with bilateral pleural plaques. He has slowly progressive breathlessness. His GP letter does not mention his work history. The respiratory consultant wants to make a firm diagnosis of asbestosis.
questions.q: Which is the most important additional step to establish the diagnosis?
questions.e: The diagnosis of asbestos-related disease rests on CT imaging combined with a thorough occupational exposure history.

steps.x: This asks about a test. Decide what you need to find out, then pick the test or result that does it.

clues: does not mention his work history
steps.x: CT is suggestive, but the exposure is not documented.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Detailed occupational exposure history.**

elim: Not needed routinely to diagnose asbestosis.

steps.x: **B. Detailed occupational exposure history.** Asbestos disease = CT + thorough occupational history.

questions.stem: A 67 year old retired builder sees his GP with 6 weeks of breathlessness and an ache in his left side. He removed asbestos roof sheets for many years. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 88 bpm, BP 134/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. He has reduced breath sounds at the left base.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: A chest X-ray is the first-line test, showing pleural plaques, fibrosis, or a unilateral effusion or pleural thickening.

steps.x: This asks about a test. Decide what you need to find out, then pick the test or result that does it.

clues: reduced breath sounds at the left base
steps.x: Asbestos worker with a possible left effusion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: First-line: **chest X-ray**.

elim: Invasive; done after imaging shows a target.
The confirmatory test for mesothelioma, not the first step.

steps.x: **A. Chest X-ray.** Asbestos-related disease: chest X-ray first, then CT.

questions.stem: A 70 year old former shipyard worker has a chest X-ray for breathlessness. It shows bilateral lower zone reticular shadowing and pleural thickening on the right that may be a mass. His oxygen saturation is 94% breathing air. He has lost 3 kg.

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Bilateral lower zone fibrosis with a right pleural-based opacity.

questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: CT chest is more sensitive than a chest X-ray for plaques, fibrosis and malignancy, and is needed to assess the possible pleural mass.

steps.x: This asks about a test. Decide what you need to find out, then pick the test or result that does it.
Fibrosis plus a possible pleural mass on plain film.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: More sensitive imaging: **CT chest**.

elim: Assesses central airways, not the pleura.
Delays assessment of a possible malignancy.

steps.x: **B. CT chest.** CT is more sensitive than CXR for plaques, fibrosis and malignancy.

questions.stem: A 75 year old man with asbestosis has 3 years of increasing breathlessness. He worked fitting asbestos insulation for 30 years. His chest has fine bibasal crackles. His oxygen saturation is 93% breathing air. Lung function tests are arranged.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on lung function testing?
o: Normal spirometry with a raised transfer factor
Restrictive pattern with reduced total lung capacity
questions.e: Fibrosis stiffens the lungs, giving a restrictive pattern: reduced FVC and total lung capacity with a normal or raised FEV1/FVC ratio.

steps.x: This asks about a test. Decide what you need to find out, then pick the test or result that does it.
Asbestosis = fibrosis = stiff, small lungs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Restrictive pattern with reduced total lung capacity.**

elim: Transfer factor is reduced in fibrosis.

steps.x: **E. Restrictive pattern with reduced total lung capacity.** Asbestosis lung function: restrictive.

questions.stem: A 69 year old former lagger has a recurrent left pleural effusion with weight loss. CT shows nodular left pleural thickening. Two pleural aspirates show an exudate, and cytology is negative for malignant cells both times. His oxygen saturation is 95% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Mesothelioma is confirmed by thoracoscopy and histology from a pleural biopsy; pleural fluid cytology is often negative.

steps.x: This asks about a test. Decide what you need to find out, then pick the test or result that does it.

clues: cytology is negative for malignant cells both times
steps.x: Suspected mesothelioma, cytology negative twice.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Tissue needed: **thoracoscopic pleural biopsy for histology**.

elim: Already negative twice; cytology often misses mesothelioma.
Does not confirm the likely malignancy.

steps.x: **D. Thoracoscopic pleural biopsy for histology.** Mesothelioma is confirmed by thoracoscopic pleural biopsy.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man who worked as an asbestos lagger and smokes 20 cigarettes a day has 2 months of cough and weight loss. CT shows a 3 cm mass in the right upper lobe with no pleural thickening. His oxygen saturation is 96% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Asbestos plus smoking markedly raises lung cancer risk; when malignancy is suspected, biopsy (bronchoscopic or CT-guided) confirms it.

steps.x: This asks about a test. Decide what you need to find out, then pick the test or result that does it.

clues: mass in the right upper lobe
steps.x: Asbestos + smoker + lung mass = likely lung cancer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Confirm with tissue: **biopsy of the lung mass**.

elim: Assess fitness but do not diagnose.
May be raised but does not confirm the cancer.
Samples the pleura, which is normal here.

steps.x: **A. Biopsy of the lung mass.** Suspected malignancy: biopsy. Pleural = thoracoscopy; lung mass = bronchoscopic or CT-guided biopsy.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man who installed asbestos lagging for 20 years has slowly progressive breathlessness. His chest X-ray shows faint lower zone shadowing. His oxygen saturation is 94% breathing air. A high-resolution CT chest is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on his CT?
o: Subpleural lower lobe fibrosis with pleural plaques
questions.e: Asbestosis on CT shows subpleural interstitial fibrosis in the lower lobes, usually with pleural plaques; CT detects this more sensitively than plain film.

steps.x: This asks about a test. Decide what you need to find out, then pick the test or result that does it.
Asbestos exposure + lower zone change = **asbestosis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Subpleural lower lobe fibrosis with pleural plaques.**
**E. Subpleural lower lobe fibrosis with pleural plaques.** Asbestosis: lower lobe fibrosis + plaques; CT more sensitive than CXR.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has bilateral pleural plaques found on a chest X-ray. He worked in a shipyard 30 years ago. He smokes 25 cigarettes a day. He is not breathless and his lung function is normal. He asks what he can do to protect his health.
questions.q: Which is the most important intervention?
questions.e: Plaques need reassurance only, but stopping smoking is vital because asbestos and smoking multiply lung cancer risk.

steps.x: This asks what to do. Work out the clinical situation first, then the step that fits it.
Benign plaques, but a smoker with asbestos exposure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Smoking cessation support.**

elim: Do not treat plaques or fibrosis.
Plaques are benign and need no surgery.

steps.x: **E. Smoking cessation support.** Asbestos + smoking is synergistic: stopping smoking matters most.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man still works in building demolition and regularly removes old insulation. He has early asbestosis on CT. He does not smoke. His oxygen saturation is 97% breathing air and he is breathless only on hills.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Continue work with a simple paper dust mask
Wear a mask only when symptoms worsen
questions.e: Further asbestos exposure must be avoided; the disease is driven by accumulated fibres and cannot be reversed.

steps.x: This asks what to do. Work out the clinical situation first, then the step that fits it.
Asbestosis, still being exposed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Avoid any further asbestos exposure.**

elim: Exposure causes harm even without symptoms.

steps.x: **A. Avoid any further asbestos exposure.** First-line: stop smoking and avoid further asbestos exposure.

questions.stem: A 78 year old woman who worked in an asbestos textile factory has advanced asbestosis. She stopped smoking 20 years ago. She is breathless at rest. Her oxygen saturation is 86% breathing air on two clinic visits 3 weeks apart. Arterial blood gas breathing air:
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
questions.e: Asbestosis is managed supportively, with oxygen therapy for chronic hypoxaemia, pulmonary rehabilitation and ongoing monitoring of lung function and imaging.

steps.x: This asks what to do. Work out the clinical situation first, then the step that fits it.

clues: 86% breathing air on two clinic visits
steps.x: Chronic hypoxaemia, non-smoker.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Supportive care: **long-term oxygen therapy**.

elim: Used in COPD or bronchiectasis with exacerbations.

steps.x: **A. Long-term oxygen therapy.** Asbestosis: supportive (oxygen, pulmonary rehab) with monitoring.

questions.stem: A 70 year old former plumber has mild asbestosis diagnosed 6 months ago. He has stopped smoking and avoids exposure. He is breathless only on stairs. His oxygen saturation is 96% breathing air. He asks what follow-up he needs.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term plan?
o: Monitoring of lung function and imaging
questions.e: Asbestosis is progressive, so supportive care with ongoing monitoring of lung function and imaging is needed; only plaques need no follow-up.

steps.x: This asks what to do. Work out the clinical situation first, then the step that fits it.
Asbestosis (not plaques), stable and mild.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Monitoring of lung function and imaging.**

elim: That applies to plaques alone, not asbestosis.

steps.x: **C. Monitoring of lung function and imaging.** Asbestosis: monitor lung function and imaging. Plaques: no follow-up.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man who worked as a shipyard lagger has biopsy-confirmed malignant pleural mesothelioma. He is fit and lives independently. His oxygen saturation is 95% breathing air. His case is being prepared for the lung cancer multidisciplinary team meeting.
questions.q: Which most determines his treatment plan?
o: The number of years since exposure
Whether he has pulmonary fibrosis on CT
questions.e: Asbestos-related malignancy is treated according to its type and stage, decided at the MDT.

steps.x: This asks what to do. Work out the clinical situation first, then the step that fits it.
Confirmed asbestos-related cancer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **The tumour type and stage.**

elim: Matters for compensation, not for choosing treatment.
Affects fitness but not the main decision.

steps.x: **D. The tumour type and stage.** Malignancy is treated by type and stage.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman with known mesothelioma is increasingly breathless over 1 week. She is now breathless at rest. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. Her left chest is stony dull to the apex. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Large left pleural effusion reaching the upper zone.

questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Mesothelioma often presents with a pleural effusion; a large symptomatic effusion should be drained to relieve breathlessness.

steps.x: This asks what to do. Work out the clinical situation first, then the step that fits it.
Large malignant effusion, very breathless.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pleural drainage.**

elim: This is a malignant effusion, not fluid overload.
Does not relieve breathlessness from the effusion now.
Drain the fluid first; it is treatable.

steps.x: **C. Pleural drainage.** Mesothelioma effusion causing breathlessness: drain it.

questions.stem: A 70 year old retired plumber has calcified pleural plaques on a chest X-ray done for a cough that has since gone. He has no breathlessness, his lung function is normal and he stopped smoking 30 years ago. He asks for a CT every year to watch the plaques.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Refer to the lung cancer clinic
questions.e: Pleural plaques are benign and are not linked to raised cancer risk, so reassurance with no follow-up is appropriate.

steps.x: This asks what to do. Work out the clinical situation first, then the step that fits it.
Plaques alone, ex-smoker, well.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Reassure with no follow-up.**

elim: Plaques do not undergo malignant change; no follow-up needed.
Plaques are benign and need no biopsy.
Plaques do not raise lung cancer risk.

steps.x: **D. Reassure with no follow-up.** Pleural plaques: reassure, no follow-up.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man has asbestosis after 25 years of fitting asbestos insulation. Lung biopsy shows asbestos fibres in the distal airways surrounded by activated macrophages, with dense interstitial fibrosis. A student asks how the fibres cause scarring.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his fibrosis?
o: Antibody-mediated destruction of alveolar basement membrane
Eosinophilic infiltration from an allergic response
Granuloma formation from a type IV hypersensitivity reaction
Macrophage release of reactive oxygen species and inflammatory mediators
questions.e: Macrophages that cannot clear the fibres release inflammatory mediators and reactive oxygen species, causing chronic inflammation and progressive fibrosis.

steps.x: This asks about the mechanism. Connect the clinical picture to the physiology underneath it.
Fibres + activated macrophages + fibrosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Macrophage release of reactive oxygen species and inflammatory mediators.**

elim: Seen in sarcoidosis or hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

steps.x: **D. Macrophage release of reactive oxygen species and inflammatory mediators.** Asbestosis: frustrated macrophages, ROS, chronic inflammation, fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 65 year old man has calcified pleural plaques on his chest X-ray from exposure 30 years ago. He is well. A student asks how inhaled fibres end up causing plaques on the chest wall and diaphragm rather than in the lung tissue.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of plaque formation?
o: Fibres migrate to the pleura and cause local irritation
Fibres trigger malignant change in mesothelial cells
Healed tuberculous infection calcifies the pleura
Lymphatic spread of carcinoma to the pleura
questions.e: Asbestos fibres migrate to and irritate the pleura, forming localised, often calcified plaques: a marker of past exposure, not a premalignant lesion.

steps.x: This asks about the mechanism. Connect the clinical picture to the physiology underneath it.
Plaques on the parietal pleura, decades after exposure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Fibres migrate to the pleura and cause local irritation.**

elim: Not the mechanism of asbestos plaques.

steps.x: **A. Fibres migrate to the pleura and cause local irritation.** Plaques = pleural irritation by migrating fibres; benign.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man who mixed asbestos for brake linings in the 1970s develops pleural mesothelioma. His employer says only white asbestos (chrysotile) was used. A review finds the factory also used blue (crocidolite) and brown (amosite) asbestos.
questions.q: Which type of fibre is most likely to have caused his mesothelioma?
questions.e: Amphibole fibres such as crocidolite and amosite are directly genotoxic to mesothelial cells, causing mutations that lead to mesothelioma after decades of latency.

steps.x: This asks about the mechanism. Connect the clinical picture to the physiology underneath it.
Mesothelioma + crocidolite and amosite exposure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Crocidolite and amosite are **amphibole fibres**.

elim: Chrysotile (serpentine) is much less carcinogenic to the mesothelium.

steps.x: **A. Amphibole fibres.** Amphiboles (blue, brown) are the most carcinogenic for mesothelioma.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man worked with asbestos insulation for 20 years and has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 40 years. He asks how his lung cancer risk compares with someone who has only one of these exposures. His lung function is mildly reduced.
questions.q: Which best describes how his two exposures combine?
o: Additive, adding the two risks together
Asbestos cancels the effect of smoking
Multiplicative, with the risks acting synergistically
No added risk once smoking is included
Smoking has no effect on asbestos-related cancer
questions.e: Smoking and asbestos act synergistically (multiplicatively) through combined carcinogenic and inflammatory pathways, so his lung cancer risk is far greater than either alone.

steps.x: This asks about the mechanism. Connect the clinical picture to the physiology underneath it.

clues: smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 40 years
how his lung cancer risk compares
steps.x: Two lung carcinogens together.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Multiplicative, with the risks acting synergistically.**

elim: The combined risk is far greater than the sum.

steps.x: **C. Multiplicative, with the risks acting synergistically.** Asbestos + smoking = multiplicative lung cancer risk: stop smoking.
